title: When text search gets faster, the refresh still has to fit

## The question

A faster text search looks like a free upgrade. The filter feels quicker and the report looks finished, while the reload that every page depends on stays out of the conversation. That reload is where the story breaks.

Power BI, Microsoft's reporting product, added full-text indexing in the September release, and you enable it on one text column at a time. Searches and filters on that text get faster, and two calculations become available, TextContains and TextSimilarity, written in DAX, the formula language. You also choose when the search index is rebuilt: during a full refresh, or during a refresh of the type Indexes, the reload whose job is the indexes. A refresh reloads the semantic model, the tables and calculations behind the report, so the pages show current data. Asking for the index makes that build part of the reload.

Chris Webb timed one of those builds this week in [Monitoring The Impact Of Full-Text Indexing On Semantic Model Refresh In Power BI](https://blog.crossjoin.co.uk/2026/10/18/monitoring-the-impact-of-full-text-indexing-on-semantic-model-refresh-in-power-bi/). His claim is the part I can use on a model that is not his: you have to test how long the index takes, because it depends on the column, and the docs warn that indexes on too many text columns can make the refresh significantly slower. The example stays a witness. On UK Land Registry Price Paid data he indexed a Street column of short names, 73,206 distinct values in a table of 160,257 rows. That index built in 1,392 milliseconds, about a second and a half, and used 484 milliseconds of processor time. I did not run his test, and I do not have his file, so that second and a half on short strings is the friendly case he measured.

The timing has to be the refresh I already run, on the model I reload for other people.

## The issue

The issue is a text column that gets a search index before anyone has timed what that index does to the refresh the report already depends on.

The person who typed a word and waited is the one a slow search annoys. Everyone who opened the page gets yesterday's numbers when the refresh runs long, and that is the failure I will be asked to explain. Webb's street names were short, and he still says a column of longer text, with more distinct values, could take a significant amount of time. He points at the docs for a sharper warning. Too many indexed text columns can slow the refresh by a lot, which is a claim about the set of columns, not the single street he timed. I have not read those docs or timed a long-text column, so his 1,392 milliseconds stays his measurement.

Webb also says Power BI reports cannot use these indexes yet. The questions he has in mind need another front end, one that can send whatever DAX query it wants. He pictures a hotel-booking model and a count of refunds for guests who complained about the air conditioning, answered with TextSimilarity. That picture is his hypothesis, and I have not built the front end. An index I turn on this week adds a refresh cost for a search my pages cannot run.

The person who loses is the one waiting on the morning reload, with a report that is already late and a new column that looks clever.

## The refresh I already run

Import models I ship store the data inside the model, which is what import mode means, so a page is current only after the reload finishes. I already wait for that reload before I treat the page as the one I will stand behind. A full-text index has to pass that same wait before it stays on.

I run that refresh twice: once with the column indexed, and once with the column left as ordinary text. The index stays only when the slower run still finishes in the time that model already takes. If either run is missing, the column stays ordinary text.

I have not enabled this feature on a model I publish, so I have no duration of my own to put next to his. A free-text comment carries a different cost, and his post already says that cost can move. Using the Land Registry figure in place of a refresh I have actually watched is how a one-column demo becomes my standard.

I already run a full refresh. A separate Indexes job would be a new schedule, another clock that can slip, and I am not adding one so the feature can hide where nobody is watching.

The comparison has to be the model I ship. A timing on a sample, or on a model that is not the one people open, approves a cost the real table never paid. Indexing several text columns and timing only the first one skips the case the docs warning is about. The refresh feels the whole set.

His trace stays in his post. He used Profiler, a recording of what the engine did during the refresh, and the 1,392 milliseconds comes from that recording. I do not run it. The duration I use is the length of the reload I already wait on, with the index and without it.

## Takeaway

A text column on a model I refresh gets a full-text index only after that same refresh, with the index on, still finishes in the time the model already takes. If I have not timed both runs, the index stays off. My reports cannot run that search yet, so an index turned on this week would add a cost and give the page nothing to use.
